opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think experimental physics is where some of the most interesting long-term changes could happen, even if they arrive a bit more slowly than on the theory side.

Right now, the thing that's surprised me most is how capable these models have become at the kind of reasoning theorists do: working through a calculation, checking symmetries, spotting where an approximation breaks down. But experiments are a different beast. They involve hardware, noise, calibration, all these messy real-world details that historically live in the heads of a few people in a lab. So in the farther future, I imagine AI becoming something like a tireless collaborator embedded in that whole loop.

One piece of that is design. When you're planning an instrument, say a next-generation telescope array or an interferometer, you face an enormous space of choices: where to put the dishes, what frequencies to observe, how to trade off sensitivity against cost. In my own area, black hole imaging, we've been thinking about space-based interferometry that could resolve the photon ring around a black hole, the thin ring of light that's orbited the hole before escaping. Designing a mission like that means simulating what the signal looks like, what the noise looks like, and whether you can actually extract the physics you care about. I can easily imagine AI systems exploring that design space far more thoroughly than a small team can, and coming back with configurations we wouldn't have thought of.

Another piece is the data itself. Modern experiments produce torrents of data, and much of the analysis is still done with pipelines humans built around what they expected to see. An AI that understands the underlying theory well enough to ask "is there something here that doesn't fit?" could be really powerful. Many discoveries in physics came from noticing a small anomaly that everyone else had dismissed as a glitch.

And then, further out, you could picture a tighter loop between theory and experiment: a system that proposes a hypothesis, works out its observable consequences, suggests the measurement that would best distinguish it from alternatives, and then helps interpret the result. That's essentially the scientific method, just running faster and with more breadth.

I'd add one caveat, though. Physics ultimately answers to nature, and somebody still has to build the thing, point it at the sky, and take the data carefully. I don't see AI replacing that. What I see is it amplifying what a single physicist or a small group can do. The kind of project that today needs a huge collaboration might, in the future, be within reach of a much smaller team. That's what excites me most: it could democratize ambitious experimental science.

r001.rationale: The response says AI reasoning currently suits theory better and experiments involve messy real-world details, but it does not attribute that difference to theory being suitable for in-silico work.

r002.rationale: It proposes AI systems exploring instrument-design choices and finding experimental configurations that a small team might miss.

r003.rationale: It describes AI helping select measurements and interpret results, but does not say AI could run complex experiments; it says people would still build the equipment and take the data.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because so much of my own work lives at the boundary between theory and what we can actually measure, especially with black holes and the Event Horizon Telescope.

In the near term, AI is already doing the unglamorous but essential things: cleaning data, calibrating instruments, finding patterns in petabytes of observations that no human could sift through. That's real, and it matters. But when I think farther out, I imagine something qualitatively different.

The first thing is instrument design. Right now, we build a telescope or a detector, and then we spend years figuring out what it can and can't tell us. I can imagine a future where you state the physical question you want to answer, and an AI system helps design the experiment from the ground up, optimizing the array configuration, the frequency coverage, the sensitivity, all against a detailed model of the expected signal and the noise. For something like a space-based interferometer to photograph the photon ring around a black hole, that kind of end-to-end design optimization could be transformative.

The second thing is closing the loop between theory and observation. Today, a theorist like me makes a prediction, an experimentalist tests it, and the feedback cycle can take a decade. I'd love to see systems that can take raw data, compare it against the full space of theoretical models in real time, and tell us not just whether general relativity holds, but exactly which measurement would discriminate most sharply between competing ideas. That turns experimental physics into something much more adaptive.

And then there's the speculative part. Physics advances when someone notices that two things nobody thought were related actually are. Whether AI can make that kind of leap, I honestly don't know. But if it can even help us see our own blind spots, show us the assumptions baked into how we analyze data, that alone would be a big deal.

What I'd caution against is thinking AI replaces the physicist. The questions still have to come from somewhere, and the judgment about what counts as a surprising result still has to come from people who understand the physics deeply. I see it as an extraordinarily powerful collaborator, not a substitute for curiosity.

r001.rationale: The response discusses theory and measurement, but does not say theoretical physics is currently a focus because it is especially suitable for work performed in silico.

r002.rationale: It proposes that AI could help design experiments from the ground up, optimizing array configuration, frequency coverage, and sensitivity.

r003.rationale: It proposes AI-assisted experiment design and analysis, but does not say AI could run highly complex physics experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think, in the farther future, AI could become a collaborator throughout the experimental process. You could imagine asking it: here’s the physics we want to probe; what measurement would distinguish these two theories? And then having it help design the experiment, figure out how to calibrate the instruments, and extract the signal from the data.

What I find especially exciting is the possibility that it could notice something we weren’t looking for. We tend to design experiments around questions we already know how to ask. An AI might help us recognize a pattern that doesn’t fit those expectations and suggest a new question.

But you’d still have to go back to nature and check. Is that pattern real? Is it an instrumental effect? Can you reproduce it independently? That’s the essential part of experimental physics. My hope is that AI will let us move much faster between an idea and a convincing test of that idea—and perhaps make experiments possible that we currently don’t know how to do.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute a current focus on theoretical physics to its suitability for in-silico work.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help design an experiment to distinguish theories and figure out how to calibrate instruments.

r003.rationale: It describes AI helping with experiment design, calibration, and data analysis, but does not propose that AI could run highly complex experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most exciting possibilities is that AI could help us design experiments, rather than just analyze the data after we’ve collected it. You could imagine giving it a scientific objective and a set of practical constraints, and asking: What measurement would best distinguish these competing ideas? What instrument would we need to make that measurement?

And then, farther down the road, you could imagine a feedback loop where an experiment takes data, the AI analyzes it, and that analysis informs what the experiment should do next. That could allow us to explore possibilities much faster.

The challenge is that finding a pattern isn’t the same as understanding the physics. We would still need ways to test what the AI proposes and establish why we should trust it. But if it can help us identify measurements or experimental designs that we wouldn’t have thought of ourselves, that could be enormously powerful.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute a current focus on theoretical physics to its suitability for in-silico work.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help design experiments by identifying useful measurements and instruments.

r003.rationale: It describes AI analyzing experimental data to inform the next step, but does not propose that AI could run highly complex physics experiments.
